match.reason: No bank point teaches solving two linear equations simultaneously by graphing or substitution and interpreting the meeting point: the closest, solving equations with graphs, covers the broader idea of reading where any two graphs meet and does not teach substitution.

draft.title: Simultaneous linear equations
card: Two linear equations that describe the same situation are called simultaneous equations. Their graphs are straight lines, and the point where the lines cross satisfies both equations.
Draw both lines on the same axes and read off the point where they cross. This is quick, but the reading may be only approximate.
Put one equation into the other to leave one unknown. Example: y = 2x + 5 and y = 3x + 1. Set 2x + 5 = 3x + 1, so x = 4. Then y = 2 × 4 + 5 = 13. The lines meet at (4, 13).
The meeting point shows where two things are equal. If two phone plans have costs C = 20 + 5t and C = 8 + 8t, they cost the same at the t-value where the lines meet.
draft.remember: The crossing point is the one pair of values that fits both equations, so both quantities are equal there.

a.q: Solve y = 2x + 1 and y = x + 6 by substitution. Where do the lines meet?
a.why: Set 2x + 1 = x + 6, so x = 5. Then y = 2 × 5 + 1 = 11, which gives (5, 11). Checking in the other equation: 5 + 6 = 11. The point (11, 5) swaps the order of x and y.
a.clue: Make the two right-hand sides equal, then find y.

b.q: Plan A costs C = 30 + 4t and Plan B costs C = 10 + 6t, where t is the number of gigabytes used. At how many gigabytes do the plans cost the same?
b.why: Set 30 + 4t = 10 + 6t, so 20 = 2t and t = 10. The cost at that point is 30 + 40 = 70 dollars, which is the answer 70, not the number of gigabytes. Check: 10 + 60 = 70.
b.clue: Ask for t, not the cost. Make the two costs equal.

check.summary: No problems found. The worked example, both answers and both explanations check out, and the card stays within this point.
